Audio Highlights July 24, 2026
articles.abstract: Listen to the JAMA Editor’s Summary for an overview and discussion of the important articles appearing in JAMA.

articles.title: US Death Rates Reach All-Time Low in 2025
articles.abstract: US death rates in 2025 were lower than ever recorded, according to provisional mortality data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

articles.title: Flu Vaccine Remains Highly Effective Against Pediatric Mortality
articles.abstract: Updated estimates of influenza vaccine effectiveness in the US found that coverage reduced the mortality risk among children and adolescents with and without underlying medical conditions.

articles.title: GLP-1 Medications May Improve Health in People With PAD and Diabetes
articles.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists may reduce hospitalizations, amputations, and deaths among people with peripheral artery disease (PAD) and type 2 diabetes compared with metformin, a new study suggests.

articles.title: FDA Approves Gene Therapy for Younger Children With Sickle Cell Disease
articles.abstract: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued supplemental approval of a gene therapy for patients aged 2 years or older with either sickle cell disease and recurrent vaso-occlusive crises or transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia.

articles.title: Metals Found in Tampons Within Margin of Safety, FDA Study Finds
articles.abstract: Metals found in tampons pose negligible toxicological concern, according to a risk assessment study at the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

articles.title: WHO Releases Global Status Report on Cancer
articles.abstract: In a new report, the World Health Organization (WHO) called for urgent action to address cancer, projecting that new cases will rise to nearly 35 million by 2050.

articles.title: Are Physicians Getting the Balance Right on Opioid Prescribing?
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses new research on opioid prescribing and use.

articles.title: Navigating the New Booming Marketplace for Menopause Care
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses how a surge in demand for menopause care has fueled a rapidly expanding marketplace of treatments and examines where the evidence supports these emerging approaches.

articles.title: Review of Gastroparesis
articles.abstract: This narrative review summarizes the pathogenesis, epidemiology, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of gastroparesis.

articles.title: How Generative AI Should Transform Clinical Decision Support
articles.abstract: This Perspective explores clinical decision support tools and which functions warrant the use of artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled large language models, including data and knowledge, delivery format, and governance.

articles.title: New Dyslipidemia Guidelines Lower the Lipid Treatment Goals and Raise the Bar for Clinical Practice
articles.abstract: New dyslipidemia guidelines from multiple US medical organizations simultaneously lowered the goals for lipid levels in many US patients and raised the bar for clinicians to help those patients reach the new goals. Among the recommendations of the more than 100-page document are the use of a new risk assessment tool (the PREVENT [Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs] score) and new lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) treatment targets, with levels as low as 70 mg/dL for most patients requiring primary prevention and as low as 55 mg/dL for most patients who are at high risk or require secondary prevention (to convert LDL-C to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0259). The new guidelines indicate that many people in the US should be candidates for lipid-lowering therapy (LLT), and many will be advised to reach new lower blood lipid concentrations.

articles.title: Dyslipidemia Evaluation and Management
articles.abstract: This JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis summarizes the 2026 American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA) guideline on management of dyslipidemia.

articles.title: Prevalence of LDL-C Above 2026 Dyslipidemia Guideline Goals Among US Adults
articles.abstract: This cross-sectional study examines the proportion of US adults whose low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels exceed 2026 guidelines across risk categories and among individuals with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

articles.title: Cardiovascular Risk Reclassification With the 2026 Dyslipidemia Guideline
articles.abstract: This study uses data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) to evaluate the extent of cardiovascular risk reclassification from the 2013 pooled cohort equations (PCEs) to the 2023 Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular EVENTs (PREVENT-ASCVD) equations.

articles.title: Review of Diagnosis and Management of Resistant Hypertension
articles.abstract: To the Editor I am writing about the recently published Review on the diagnosis and management of resistant hypertension. While acknowledging the clinical relevance and clarity of the Review, there are 3 key aspects that I believe warrant further discussion: (1) the definition and clinical significance of controlled resistant hypertension, (2) the important role of diagnostic pathways in distinguishing true from apparent resistant hypertension, and (3) the need for a more adaptable, phenotype-informed approach to fourth-line therapy in light of emerging evidence.

articles.title: Review of Diagnosis and Management of Resistant Hypertension
articles.abstract: To the Editor A recent Review provided practical information about resistant hypertension. One point that may merit clarification is how the differing US and European diagnostic thresholds should be translated into decisions about renal denervation. The Review noted that US guidance defines resistant hypertension as office blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or greater, whereas European guidelines define it as 140/90 mm Hg or greater, with different ambulatory thresholds as well. Yet the sham-controlled renal denervation evidence summarized in the Review is derived largely from trials enrolling patients at or above the higher threshold; in the cited meta-analysis, 9 of 10 trials required office blood pressure of at least 140/90 mm Hg, and only 4 explicitly required a diagnosis of resistant hypertension. Could the authors clarify whether the renal denervation branch in their treatment algorithm is intended to apply to patients who meet the lower US definition alone or primarily to patients whose blood pressure profile resembles that of the device trial populations? A more explicit linkage between diagnostic definitions and the populations studied in renal denervation trials would help clinicians judge referral timing without overstating the current evidence base.

articles.title: Review of Diagnosis and Management of Resistant Hypertension
articles.abstract: To the Editor We read with interest the recent comprehensive Review on the management of resistant hypertension. We have concerns, however, about a disconnect between the article’s evidence and the article’s Abstract conclusion, which seemed to equate the efficacy of spironolactone and renal denervation. Elevating renal denervation to the same level as spironolactone is not endorsed by the 2025 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology high blood pressure guidelines. In fact, these guidelines discuss renal denervation as a potential consideration only after mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.

articles.title: Review of Diagnosis and Management of Resistant Hypertension—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We appreciate the letters about our Review and agree that several aspects of resistant hypertension warrant further clarification.

articles.title: Implications of the 2026 Dyslipidemia Guideline for Primary Prevention Statin Therapy
articles.abstract: This cross-sectional study explores the 2026 guideline on dyslipidemia management, examining the population health impact on US adults recommended primary prevention statin therapy due to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk.

articles.title: Consecratio Medici
articles.abstract: Harvey Cushing, M.D., Boston

articles.title: Lead Exposure and the Coronary Heart Disease Epidemic
articles.abstract: To the Editor A recent Editorial compellingly reframed coronary heart disease (CHD) as, in part, the vascular imprint of industrial lead exposure, challenging decades of risk attribution centered on individual behaviors. As estimates of lead-attributable cardiovascular burden expand, this perspective has important implications for prevention. An additional dimension, however, warrants consideration: how toxicologic burden is measured and operationalized within clinical and public health systems.

articles.title: Lead Exposure and the Coronary Heart Disease Epidemic—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply In their Letter about my recent Editorial, Dr Yuan and colleagues rightly identify a central limitation in how the contribution of lead to CHD is estimated. We rely heavily on population-level models that fail to capture the cumulative, interactive effects of multiple risk factors—lead, air pollution, cadmium, arsenic, diet, tobacco smoke, and more recently identified exposures such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances and microplastics. Even this likely understates the true burden, as these exposures contribute to CHD and a range of conditions across the life course, including preterm birth, cognitive deficits, and kidney disease.

articles.title: Would Anyone Notice?
articles.abstract: In this narrative medicine essay, a psychiatric residency program director ponders a resident’s surprise utterance after her program directors went so far as to drive to her home when she missed a shift after not being able to be reached by phone or text message.

articles.title: Tumor Debulking Plus Chemotherapy for Multiorgan Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
articles.abstract: To the Editor We welcome the report of the ORCHESTRA randomized clinical trial (RCT) that investigated the effect on overall survival from debulking of metastases after first-line systemic treatment in patients with stage 4 CRC. The trial reported no difference between the 2 groups for the primary outcome of overall survival. PulMiCC, a phase 3 RCT of surgical resection of CRC lung metastases, reached the same conclusion, but, surprisingly, Dr Gootjes and colleagues did not mention it. The editorialist opined that “ORCHESTRA hits a sour note.” We take a contrary view: ORCHESTRA rings true.

articles.title: Tumor Debulking Plus Chemotherapy for Multiorgan Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
articles.abstract: To the Editor The ORCHESTRA trial addressed the evolving role of local therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). The authors should be commended for their rigorous evaluation of debulking in this challenging setting. The study required that patients have metastases in at least 2 different organs. However, patients had metastatic sites with very different prognoses (eg, lungs, bone, peritoneum). In such widely disseminated disease, progression of the less favorable site inevitably determines survival. We are concerned that the induction systemic therapy was brief—only 3 to 4 cycles—using only capecitabine and oxaliplatin with or without bevacizumab or folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin with or without bevacizumab. Given advanced metastatic disease, these regimens appear insufficient to reliably ensure good control of the systemic disease. Compounding this issue, patients who achieved merely stable disease (vs an objective response) were included. To select candidates who might genuinely benefit from local therapies, a longer induction period leading to a sustained objective response to chemotherapy for a period of at least 3 months is essential.

articles.title: Tumor Debulking Plus Chemotherapy for Multiorgan Metastatic Colorectal Cancer—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We appreciate the comments raised by Dr Adam and colleagues; their comments do not undermine the outcome of the ORCHESTRA study. We fully acknowledge the role of debulking surgery in more limited metastatic disease confined to the liver.

articles.title: Distance Learning
articles.abstract: My mother asks on the phone if I’ve eaten the way she asked when I still lived close enough to lie convincingly. Now three time zones sit between us and I measure the distance not in miles but in meals I’ve missed at her table.

articles.title: Choosing Distance: Medical Professionalism and Poetry
articles.abstract: Poetry, through its visceral immediacy and catalyzing of human emotion, has the power to close distances. Many argue that recent technological advancement has created the opposite, a loss of interpersonal connection, but the experience of alienation or simply growing apart is innate to the human condition, sometimes necessarily accompanying personal growth. In fact, developing professional relationships within health care has long grappled with fostering appropriate distance between physicians and patients, who share intimate, health-related details of their lives, or among physician colleagues, who often witness stressful events together but ultimately must confront such burdens alone. The poem “Distance Learning” provides an example of a clinician in training questioning distance, although ironically not the type enforced by the hospital workplace setting. Instead, the speaker remarks on “a distance I chose” from her own family in seeking medical training. Using tender, homespun imagery juxtaposed against her rigorous hospital duties, the realities of her vocation strain against the comforts of sitting around a familiar table, being with caring parents, and experiencing uninterrupted, unabashed closeness with her loved ones. The poem acknowledges that problematic, well-known ethos in medicine that career always takes priority—physicians must eat, drink, and sleep medicine—creating tension between its duties and physicians’ other needs and interests. Yet in a poem that elicits the pains and sacrifices of pursuing medical training, we still find an accessible, paradoxically forgiving space that helps bridge emotional distance when physical closeness seems impossible.

articles.title: Cutting Medicaid for Children
articles.abstract: This Viewpoint discusses reductions in Medicaid spending due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and how these cuts could affect US children’s health insurance coverage, leading to long-term financial repercussions.

articles.title: Patient Information: Low Back Pain
articles.abstract: This JAMA Patient Page describes the common symptoms of nonspecific low back pain, the diagnosis and treatment, and the prognosis.

articles.title: Addressing Multimorbidity Challenges in Diabetes
articles.abstract: The prevalence of diabetes continues to increase in the US: approximately 40 million people have diabetes, and 115 million adults aged 18 years or older have prediabetes. More than 30 million adults with prediabetes are aged 65 years or older and more than half of these older adults (52.1%) are at risk of diabetes and multimorbidity. Worldwide, data from the International Diabetes Federation suggest that in 2024 more than 500 million adults were living with diabetes, and this number is projected to increase to close to 900 million by 2050. Adding individuals with prediabetes, a previous analysis of the International Diabetes Federation Diabetes Atlas reported that prediabetes affected approximately 720 million individuals worldwide, with nearly 1 billion people with prediabetes projected by 2045.

articles.title: Lifestyle and Metformin Interventions and Risk of Multimorbidity in Adults With Prediabetes
articles.abstract: This trial examines lifestyle and metformin interventions and risk of multimorbidity in adults with prediabetes.

articles.title: Precision, Pragmatism, and Emerging Paradigms in Determining Kidney Filtration Function
articles.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined largely by glomerular filtration rate (GFR), a construct with broad clinical implications. Guidelines from Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes categorize CKD stages in adults according to GFR thresholds and albuminuria to assess risk of kidney failure. These CKD categories help clinicians dose medications with a narrow therapeutic window (eg, chemotherapy, antimicrobials), screen for metabolic complications of kidney dysfunction, determine eligibility for kidney transplant, and evaluate risks of death and cardiovascular disease events. Yet a patient’s GFR assessment depends on which test is ordered. In routine clinical practice, GFR is estimated (eGFR) rather than measured (mGFR). Small differences between estimates for GFR that fall close to the thresholds for CKD categorization can reclassify a patient’s disease status, thereby influencing diagnostic testing and treatment decisions. Measured GFR is the reference standard, but it is burdensome, time consuming, and not widely available. Thus, most clinical studies rely on eGFR to determine the associations of CKD with kidney failure, cardiovascular disease, and death.

articles.title: Measured and Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rates and Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes
articles.abstract: This study evaluates associations between major clinical outcomes and measured glomerular filtration rate (GFR), estimated GFR (eGFR) for plasma creatinine, eGFR for cystatin C, and eGFR for a combination of plasma creatinine and cystatin C in a large cohort of patients in Sweden.
